'''Benjamin Franklin Peery Jr.,''' (4 March 1922 - 30 November 2010) was an American physicist, astronomer, and longtime professor at [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]] and [[Howard University]]. He was the second African American person to receive a doctorate in astronomy.<ref name=":0" />

== Early life and military service ==
Benjamin F. Peery was born on 4 March 1922 in [[St. Joseph, Missouri]], to Benjamin Peery Sr., and Caroline Watkins Peery, and was the oldest of seven brothers.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Physics |first=American Institute of |date=2021-09-24 |title=Benjamin Peery |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/33698 |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=www.aip.org |language=en}}</ref> His father was a railway mail clerk and wrote for the Twin Cities Herald, and his mother was a school teacher. His younger brother, [[Nelson Peery]], was a political activist and author. The Peery family moved frequently for Benjamin Peery, Sr.'s line of work, eventually settling in southeast Minnesota. The Peerys lived in [[Randolph, Minnesota]]; [[Wabasha, Minnesota]]; and eventually [[Minneapolis|Minneapolis, Minnesota]], where Peery attended and graduated high school. Prior to attending college, he worked as a draftsman.

After one year of college, in 1942 Peery joined the [[United States Army Air Forces|Army Air Force]], in which he served from 1942 until 1945, participating in campaigns in Italy and North Africa.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Cowley |first=Charles R. |date=2011-01-31 |title=Benjamin Franklin Peery (1922–2010) |url=https://baas.aas.org/pub/benjamin-franklin-peery-1922-2010/release/2 |journal=Bulletin of the AAS |language=en |volume=43 |issue=1}}</ref>

== Education ==
Peery attended the [[University of Minnesota]] as an undergraduate for one year before joining the military. After completing his service, he returned to the university on the [[G.I. Bill]] to complete his studies. After receiving his bachelor's degree in physics in 1949, he worked as a physics instructor for two years at [[North Carolina A&T State University]].<ref name=":1" />

Peery then attended [[Fisk University]] in [[Nashville, Tennessee]], where he received a master's degree in physics in 1955. His master's thesis involved the study of infra-red spectrum and structure of PO C13. He then continued his graduate studies at the [[University of Michigan]], completing a doctorate in astronomy in 1962. His thesis was titled "The system VV cephei," and his doctoral advisor was [[Dean Benjamin McLaughlin]]. His thesis work was supported in part by a University Fellowship that Peery was awarded between 1958 and 1959.<ref>{{cite thesis |id={{ProQuest|302109121}} |last1=Peery |first1=Benjamin F. |date=1962 |title=The system VV cephei }}</ref>

Some of his fellow students at Michigan included [[Edward Spiegel]], [[Martha Locke Hazen|Martha Hazen]], Arthur Upgren and Lowell Doherty. He also studied under Leo Goldberg, Freeman Miller, and [[Lawrence H. Aller]].<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
In 1959, while still completing his doctorate, Peery began teaching at [[Indiana University]], and accepted a position there as assistant professor of astronomy in 1962. In 1968 he was appointed associate professor with permanent tenure and in 1973 was promoted to full professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Benjamin F. Peery's Astronomical Influence on IU – Voices from the IU Bicentennial |url=https://blogs.iu.edu/bicentennialblogs/2020/04/08/dr-benjamin-f-peerys-astronomical-influence-on-iu/ |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=blogs.iu.edu}}</ref> While at Indiana, Peery was active in research and helped to add a 16-inch telescope to the [[Morgan-Monroe State Forest Station of the Goethe Link Observatory|Morgan-Monroe State Forest Station of the Goethe Link Observatories]] near   [[Martinsville, Indiana]]. He also worked with the [[National Science Teaching Association|National Science Teachers Association's]] (ASTA) Elementary School Science Program. In 1975–1976, he took a sabbatical leave to conduct research at [[Kitt Peak National Observatory]] in [[Tucson, Arizona]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Drabelle |first=Dennis |date=1992-08-02 |title=ASTRONOMER IN THE CLASSROOM |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/entertainment/books/1992/08/02/astronomer-in-the-classroom/2cebfaf4-0f5a-4225-88f8-1114f9a74621/ |access-date=2023-05-08 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

In 1977, he left Indiana for a position at [[Howard University]], where he had been recruited to start an astrophysics graduate program. There, he became chair of the physics and astrophysics departments. At this point, it was estimated that Peery was one of only five Black astronomers in the United States.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ltd |first=Earl G. Graves |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iAJYrOAJGNUC&dq=benjamin+peery&pg=PA28 |title=Black Enterprise |date=February 1977 |publisher=Earl G. Graves, Ltd. |language=en}}</ref> He remained at Howard University until 1992, when he retired and became an emeritus professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=JBHE: Latest News for 1/20/11 |url=https://www.jbhe.com/latest/news/1-20-11/memoriam.html |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=www.jbhe.com}}</ref> While at Howard, he also took two years' leave at the [[National Science Foundation]] to serve as its program director for the astronomy division.<ref name=":2" />

In 1991, Peery was featured in episode five of the [[PBS]] documentary "The Astronomers."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brennan |first=Patricia |date=1991-04-14 |title='THE ASTRONOMERS' |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/tv/1991/04/14/the-astronomers/510bc7d0-bfaf-4b9a-b2e0-9436762e6bc3/ |access-date=2023-05-08 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Over the course of his career, he was also a member of several professional organizations, including: the [[International Astronomical Union]];<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Astronomical Union {{!}} IAU |url=https://www.iau.org/administration/membership/individual/3417/ |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=www.iau.org}}</ref> the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]]; the [[American Astronomical Society]]; the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]; and as a trustee of the [[Adler Planetarium]] in [[Chicago|Chicago, Illinois]]. He also conducted research at [[Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory]] in Chile, and was a visiting professor at [[Harvard University]], the [[California Institute of Technology]] and the [[College of William & Mary|College of William and Mary]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0" />

== Research ==
While at Indiana, Peery designed and constructed one of the first oscilloscope measuring engines, which was referred to colloquially as "the Peeryscope." His early research centered on cool giant stars and, but later progressed to the chemical makeup of stars, including systems in which the radioactive element technetium could be identified in the spectrum.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /> His research has also included the physics of stellar structure, evolution and nucleosynthesis, and the physics of interacting binary stars.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Benjamin F. Peery - Physicist of the African Diaspora |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/peery_benjaminf.html |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Peery is the namesake of the Benjamin F. Peery Jr. Diversity Award, a graduate scholarship at [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scholarships + Awards |url=https://astro.indiana.edu/about/alumni-giving/scholarships-awards.html |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=Department of Astronomy |language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Peery was married to Darnelle Macklin Peery, a special education teacher, whom he met while a student at [[Fisk University]]. They had one daughter, Yvany Peery, who is a psychotherapist.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Brown |first=Emma |date=2010-12-24 |title=Benjamin F. Peery, Howard University astronomer, dies at 88 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US |url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/12/23/AR2010122304395.html |access-date=2023-05-05 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>
